title: ORA-00054 Resource Busy in Oracle: Causes and Fixes
description: Fix ORA-00054 resource busy in Oracle: find the session holding the lock, use DDL_LOCK_TIMEOUT and ONLINE builds, and handle NOWAIT in PL/SQL.

sources.title: Oracle 19c SQL Reference: ALTER SYSTEM (KILL SESSION)
Oracle 19c Administrator's Guide: Managing Indexes (online builds)
Oracle 19c Concepts: Data Concurrency and Consistency

reviewNotes: Examples written from the 19c docs and not run; please test in two sessions on 19c (and 23ai/26ai if possible). Check: (1) the exact ORA-00054 text on 23ai/26ai, since the error help page lists a newer 'Failed to acquire a lock...' form; (2) that non-ONLINE CREATE INDEX and ALTER TABLE ADD fail with ORA-00054 while another session has uncommitted DML (general Oracle knowledge, not stated on a fetched page); (3) the claim that online index builds need brief locks at start and end and wait on open transactions, and that ONLINE builds are Enterprise Edition only (from general knowledge, not a fetched page); (4) the warning that DML can queue behind a waiting DDL; (5) that FOR UPDATE WAIT n raises ORA-30006 on timeout; (6) the SQL*Plus error layout with the asterisk under TRUNCATE. SID/SERIAL# values in outputs are illustrative. The 'DDL_LOCK_TIMEOUT from 11g' claim comes from third-party pages (Datavail, Doyensys); the 19c parameter page does not state the release.

data.text: ORA-00054: resource busy and acquire with NOWAIT specified or timeout expired means your statement needed a lock that another session already holds, and Oracle was told not to wait for it (or waited and gave up). It usually hits DDL such as TRUNCATE, ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE or CREATE INDEX while someone has uncommitted changes on the same table.

The fix is almost never "run it again and hope". You find the session holding the lock, decide whether it should finish or be stopped, and then either let your DDL wait with DDL_LOCK_TIMEOUT or use an online operation that does not need an exclusive lock for long. This guide shows each step with a small example you can run in two SQL*Plus or SQL Developer sessions.
What ORA-00054 means

Every INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE takes a table-level DML lock (a TM lock) in row exclusive mode. This lock lets other sessions keep changing other rows, so normal OLTP work does not notice it. It is held until the transaction commits or rolls back.

Most DDL needs a much stronger lock on the table. Oracle cannot truncate or restructure a table while another transaction still has uncommitted changes in it. So the DDL has to get past those TM locks first.

By default, DDL does not queue behind DML locks. DDL_LOCK_TIMEOUT defaults to 0, and the Oracle Reference says a value of zero means NOWAIT. So the DDL checks once, sees the lock, and fails straight away with ORA-00054.
The same error appears when you ask for NOWAIT yourself:

content: TRUNCATE, DROP, ALTER TABLE, CREATE INDEX (without ONLINE)
DDL needs an exclusive lock and DDL_LOCK_TIMEOUT is 0 by default
Any DDL with DDL_LOCK_TIMEOUT set above 0
It waited for the set number of seconds and the lock was still held
You told Oracle not to wait for the table lock
You told Oracle not to wait for locked rows

data.title: Newer message text
data.text: The classic text is the one above. The current Oracle error help page also lists a more detailed form that starts "Failed to acquire a lock ... because it is currently held by another session" and names the resource. The cause is the same either way. Note that SELECT ... FOR UPDATE WAIT n raises a different error when the wait runs out: ORA-30006.
Sample setup
Create a small orders table. You need two sessions connected as the same user. Call them Session A and Session B.

data.caption: Run once in either session

data.text: Reproduce ORA-00054 in two sessions
Step 1: leave a transaction open in Session A

data.code:
-- Session A
UPDATE orders
   SET status = 'PAID'
 WHERE order_id = 1;

-- no COMMIT yet
data.caption: Session A holds a row lock and a TM lock on ORDERS

data.text: Session A now holds a lock on row 1 and a row exclusive TM lock on the whole ORDERS table. Nothing looks wrong yet. Other sessions can still read every row and update rows 2, 3 and 4.
Step 2: run DDL in Session B

data.caption: Session B tries to empty the table

data.code:
TRUNCATE TABLE orders
               *
ERROR at line 1:
ORA-00054: resource busy and acquire with NOWAIT specified or timeout expired
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: Session B failed immediately. It did not wait, because DDL_LOCK_TIMEOUT is 0. If Session A commits or rolls back and Session B runs the same TRUNCATE again, it succeeds.

Try ALTER TABLE orders ADD (note VARCHAR2(100)); or CREATE INDEX orders_cust_ix ON orders (customer); in Session B while Session A is still open. In the usual case you get the same ORA-00054, because both need to get past Session A's lock.
Find the session that holds the lock

V$LOCKED_OBJECT lists the DML (TM) locks held by every transaction, with the object ID and the session ID. Join it to DBA_OBJECTS for the table name and to V$SESSION for who the session is and what it is doing. You need SELECT access on these views, which DBAs have by default.

data.code:
SELECT lo.session_id        AS sid,
       s.serial#,
       s.username,
       s.status,
       s.machine,
       s.program,
       o.owner,
       o.object_name,
       DECODE(lo.locked_mode,
              2, 'ROW SHARE',
              3, 'ROW EXCLUSIVE',
              4, 'SHARE',
              5, 'SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE',
              6, 'EXCLUSIVE',
              TO_CHAR(lo.locked_mode)) AS lock_mode,
       s.last_call_et      AS seconds_since_last_call
  FROM v$locked_object lo
  JOIN dba_objects     o ON o.object_id = lo.object_id
  JOIN v$session       s ON s.sid       = lo.session_id
 WHERE o.object_name = 'ORDERS'
   AND o.owner       = USER;
data.caption: Who holds a lock on ORDERS?

data.text: Output (expected output). Your SID, SERIAL#, machine and program values will differ.

Read it like this. Session 142 holds a ROW EXCLUSIVE lock on ORDERS, which is what an uncommitted UPDATE leaves behind. Its status is INACTIVE, which means it is not running anything right now. It ran its last statement 95 seconds ago and then stopped. This is the classic cause of ORA-00054: someone ran DML in a tool and did not commit.
If you run this on Oracle RAC, use GV$LOCKED_OBJECT and GV$SESSION and join on inst_id as well, because the holder may be on another instance.
See what the holding session ran
V$SESSION has SQL_ID for the current statement and PREV_SQL_ID for the previous one. An idle session usually has no current statement, so look at the previous one.

data.code:
SELECT s.sid, q.sql_text
  FROM v$session s
  JOIN v$sql     q ON q.sql_id = s.prev_sql_id
 WHERE s.sid = 142
   AND ROWNUM = 1;
data.caption: Last SQL the holder ran

content: UPDATE orders SET status = 'PAID' WHERE order_id = 1

data.text: Output (expected output). This is only the last statement, not the whole transaction. The session may have changed other tables earlier. Still, it usually tells you which application or person to contact.

data.title: Already have a blocking session query?
data.text: ORA-00054 is the "no wait" side of normal lock blocking. If your DDL was waiting instead of failing, the waiting session shows up in V$SESSION.BLOCKING_SESSION. See the Oracle blocking sessions query guide for that approach.
How to fix ORA-00054
Pick the fix based on who holds the lock and how urgent your DDL is. Work down this list from the safest option.
Fix 1: let the holder commit or roll back

If the holder is a person in SQL Developer or a batch job that is about to finish, ask them to commit or roll back, or wait for the job. Then run your DDL again. Nothing is lost and nobody's work is undone.

data.caption: After the holder commits

data.text: Fix 2: make the DDL wait with DDL_LOCK_TIMEOUT

DDL_LOCK_TIMEOUT sets how many seconds DDL waits in the DML lock queue before it gives up. It is available from Oracle 11g. The range is 0 to 1,000,000 seconds, and per the docs the maximum value means wait forever. Set it at session level for your maintenance script, not system-wide.

data.caption: Wait up to 60 seconds for the lock

data.text: Now Session B waits instead of failing. If Session A commits within 60 seconds, the TRUNCATE runs at that moment. If not, Session B gets ORA-00054 after 60 seconds, which is the "timeout expired" part of the message.

This is the right fix when the table is busy with short transactions. Each transaction holds its lock for a moment, and your DDL slips in between them. It does not help when a session has been idle with an open transaction for an hour.

data.title: A waiting DDL can block others
data.text: While your DDL waits for its exclusive lock, new DML on that table can queue behind it. On a busy table, a long timeout can make application sessions hang until your DDL finishes or gives up. Use a short timeout and run maintenance in quiet hours.
Fix 3: use an online operation
For indexes, use the ONLINE keyword. The Oracle Administrator's Guide says you can run DML on the base table while an online index build is taking place.

data.code:
CREATE INDEX orders_cust_ix ON orders (customer) ONLINE;

ALTER INDEX orders_cust_ix REBUILD ONLINE;
data.caption: Online index build and rebuild

data.text: An online build still needs short table locks at the start and the end. If a transaction stays open for a long time, the online build waits for it rather than failing, so combine ONLINE with Fix 1 when a session has been idle for a long time. Online index builds are an Enterprise Edition feature.
Fix 4: end the holding session (last resort)

If the holder is an abandoned session, for example a laptop that went to sleep with an open transaction, a DBA can end it. Oracle rolls back its uncommitted work and releases its locks. Confirm with the owner first. Their changes are lost.

data.code:
-- Use SID and SERIAL# from the V$LOCKED_OBJECT query
ALTER SYSTEM KILL SESSION '142,31877' IMMEDIATE;
data.caption: Kill the session that holds the lock

data.text: IMMEDIATE tells Oracle to roll back, release locks and return control to you at once. A large transaction can still take time to roll back, and its locks stay until the rollback finishes. A gentler option is ALTER SYSTEM DISCONNECT SESSION '142,31877' POST_TRANSACTION;, which lets the current transaction complete before disconnecting. That only helps if the session is actually going to finish.
Handle ORA-00054 in PL/SQL

Sometimes you want NOWAIT on purpose. A screen that edits an order should tell the user "someone else is editing this" instead of hanging. Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT and catch the error. ORA-00054 has no predefined exception name, so give it one with PRAGMA EXCEPTION_INIT.

data.caption: Lock the row or report that it is busy

data.text: Run this in Session B while Session A still has row 1 locked, with SET SERVEROUTPUT ON:

data.code:
Order 1 is being edited by another session. Try again later.

PL/SQL procedure successfully completed.
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: If you prefer a short wait, use FOR UPDATE WAIT 5. Then the error after 5 seconds is ORA-30006, not ORA-00054, so map -30006 as well. For queue tables where any free row will do, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED skips locked rows instead of failing.
For DDL inside PL/SQL, such as a nightly EXECUTE IMMEDIATE TRUNCATE, set DDL_LOCK_TIMEOUT first and then catch -54 so the job logs a clear message rather than failing with an unhandled error.

data.caption: Nightly truncate with a timeout (orders_stage is an example table)

data.text: Common mistakes

items.content: Retrying in a loop without looking. If the holder is an idle session with an open transaction, it will hold the lock until someone ends it. Find it with V$LOCKED_OBJECT first.

Forgetting your own other session. Very often the holder is you, in another SQL Developer tab or worksheet with an uncommitted UPDATE. Check the USERNAME and MACHINE columns before you contact anyone else.

Setting DDL_LOCK_TIMEOUT system-wide. ALTER SYSTEM SET ddl_lock_timeout makes every session's DDL wait, including deployments that you would rather fail fast. Set it per session in the script that needs it.
Killing sessions without asking. Killing rolls back someone's uncommitted work. On production, that may be a payment or a batch that has run for an hour.
Expecting COMMIT in another session to help. Only the session that holds the lock can release it by committing or rolling back. Running COMMIT in your own session does nothing for theirs.

Thinking TRUNCATE is "just a fast DELETE". TRUNCATE is DDL. It commits, it needs an exclusive lock and it cannot be rolled back. If you only need to remove rows while users are working, DELETE waits for row locks instead of failing.

data.text: Best practices to avoid ORA-00054

items.content: Commit or roll back promptly in interactive tools. An open transaction in a forgotten worksheet is the most common cause.
Put ALTER SESSION SET ddl_lock_timeout = n at the top of deployment and maintenance scripts, with n between 10 and 60 seconds as a starting point you adjust for your system.
Use CREATE INDEX ... ONLINE and ALTER INDEX ... REBUILD ONLINE on tables that users are writing to.
Schedule DDL on busy tables in a quiet window, and check V$LOCKED_OBJECT for the table just before you start.
In applications, use FOR UPDATE NOWAIT or WAIT n where a user is waiting on screen, and handle the error with a friendly message.
Do not hold transactions open while waiting for user input or for a remote call to finish.

data.text: Frequently asked questions
How do I resolve ORA-00054 resource busy?

Find the session holding a lock on the table with V$LOCKED_OBJECT joined to V$SESSION. Ask it to commit or roll back, or set DDL_LOCK_TIMEOUT so your DDL waits. End the session with ALTER SYSTEM KILL SESSION only as a last resort.
Why does TRUNCATE give ORA-00054?

TRUNCATE is DDL and needs an exclusive lock on the table. If any other session has uncommitted DML on it, the lock is not available, and with the default DDL_LOCK_TIMEOUT of 0 the TRUNCATE fails at once instead of waiting.
How do I release a lock on a table in Oracle?

Oracle has no statement that removes another session's lock. Locks are released when the transaction that holds them commits or rolls back. If that session is gone or abandoned, killing it makes Oracle roll back its work and release the locks.
What is DDL_LOCK_TIMEOUT in Oracle?

It is an initialization parameter, available from Oracle 11g, that sets how many seconds DDL waits for a DML lock before raising ORA-00054. The default is 0 (no wait), the maximum is 1,000,000 seconds, and you can change it with ALTER SESSION or ALTER SYSTEM.
Does ORA-00054 happen with CREATE INDEX?

Yes. A normal CREATE INDEX needs to lock the table against DML and fails with ORA-00054 if another transaction has uncommitted changes on it. Use CREATE INDEX ... ONLINE so DML can continue during the build.
Summary

items.content: ORA-00054 means another session holds a lock you need and your statement did not wait (or the wait timed out).
Reproduce it: uncommitted UPDATE in one session, TRUNCATE or ALTER in another.
Find the holder with V$LOCKED_OBJECT + DBA_OBJECTS + V$SESSION, and check PREV_SQL_ID to see what it ran.
Prefer asking the holder to commit or roll back over killing the session.
Use ALTER SESSION SET ddl_lock_timeout for maintenance scripts, and keep the timeout short.
Use ONLINE for index builds and rebuilds on busy tables.
Handle intentional NOWAIT with PRAGMA EXCEPTION_INIT(e, -54); FOR UPDATE WAIT n raises ORA-30006 instead.

linkedin.post:
Your TRUNCATE fails in one second with ORA-00054, but nobody seems to be using the table.

Here is what is happening and how to fix it.

→ Some session has an uncommitted UPDATE, INSERT or DELETE on that table. Often it is your own other SQL Developer tab.

→ DDL needs an exclusive lock, and DDL_LOCK_TIMEOUT is 0 by default. So Oracle does not wait, it fails at once.

→ Find the holder: join V$LOCKED_OBJECT to DBA_OBJECTS and V$SESSION. An INACTIVE session with a ROW EXCLUSIVE lock is the usual cause.

→ Let your script wait a little: ALTER SESSION SET ddl_lock_timeout = 30;

→ For indexes on busy tables, use CREATE INDEX ... ONLINE so DML can continue.

Kill the session only as a last resort. Its uncommitted work is rolled back.

In PL/SQL, map the error with PRAGMA EXCEPTION_INIT(e_busy, -54) when you use FOR UPDATE NOWAIT on purpose.

What do you do first when ORA-00054 hits a production deployment: wait, retry or kill?
